maintopic: AUTOMATIC GRAIN-WEIGHERS IN THE NORTH-WEST TERRITORIES.
speechtext:
I regret that when the House was discussing this matter yesterday, the hour for recess arrived, and cut off the debate. A couple of minutes would have sufficed me to say all I wished to say in support of the contention of my hon. friend from Lis-gar (Mr. Stewart). I regret also that the facts of the matter are such as compel me to endorse the remarks that were made by the hon. gentleman from Lisgar (Mr. Stewart) and the future remarks made even more vehemently by my hon. friend from Macdonald (Mr. Boyd). The question is one of considerable importance to the grain growing sections between Lake Superior and the Rocky Mountains. The fact is becoming emphasized in various ways that Canada is a large country. Western Canada itself is a large country, and the wheat growing industry of western Canada has become a very important enterprise. The grain products west of Lake Superior now exceed annually one hundred million bushels. This fact in itself is the testimony that the industry has become a very important one. The industry of threshing out these large crops of grain is also a very important one, and it is found that the method which has been employed in times past, the method of weighing or measuring the threshed grain has become obsolete and impossible. In Manitoba and the North-west Territories, the conditions have led to the invention of an automatic weighing device which to-day is a necessity, and although the device is not a legalized instrument for weighing or measuring, the threshers and farmers in that country are compelled to use it. The fact that this device has not been legalized, and the further fact that it has been necessary to use it for some years, have led to a considerable

amount of litigation both in Manitoba and the North-west Territories. Cases have been taken in Manitoba by the threshers to collect accounts against farmers for threshing, and the decisions have been given to the effect that where this automatic weighing device has been used the threshers cannot legally collect their accounts. In reality all the threshers of that country are now dependent for their pay upon the honour and good faith of the individual farmer.
Cases have also been taken in the Northwest Territories and the decision of one trial judge was similar to the Manitoba decision. But, last fall, I may say, the Attorney General's Department of the North-west Territories took up one of the cases and obtained a decision from the appeal court to the effect that if the grain was measured in a bin where the bin was so constructed that the cubic measurement could be obtained, the thresher could legally collect his bill from the farmer. Still that is only in a few cases practicable, so that in the North-west Territories and Manitoba, the automatic weighing device not being legalized, the threshers is at the mercy of the individual farmer for the collection of his account. As was stated yesterday afternoon, the representatives from Manitoba and the North-west Territories were, a year ago. invited to go over to the Inland Revenue Department to witness tests being made of this automatic weighing device, and I, with others from the west, was over on two or three occasions. The device was very thoroughly tested over there and tested to the satisfaction of all of us and we understood that it met with the satisfaction too of the officers of the Inland Revenue Department. Up to the present time the sanction of the department has not been given to the adoption of this automatic weigher. In asking that the department give legal sanction to the weigher, we are not asking anything which will endanger or harm any interest or any persons. The machine is satisfactory to the thresher and it is satisfactory to the farmer. It is approximately, and I believe absolutely, accurate. Farmers have told me that the results in the elevator, where there is a legalized weighing scale, tally aproximately accurately with the results given by the automatic weigher. I simply wish to join the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Stewart) and the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Boyd) in urging the matter upon the attention of the House and particularly on the attention of the hon. Minister of Inland Revenue.
hon. gentlemen representing constituencies in Manitoba and the North-west Territories to confer with me on matters relating to the weighing of grain. In June last, as the correspondence will show, one of the officers of the department, Mr. Magness, of Winnipeg, inspector of weights and measures, wrote to the department, stating that he thought he had invented a machine which would be satisfactory to both the owners of threshing machines and to the farmers and that he thought this machine should be admitted to verification. I ordered immediately that Mr. Magness should come down to Ottawa, bringing with him the machine which he lmd invented. The machine was tested and I must say that after the trial one of the officers of the department, who had no special authority either to examine or verify, wrote a certain letter which will be brought down with the other documents. Later on, in order not to put farmers and owners of threshing machines to the necessity of engaging in new litigation, we brought here an expert, and I must say to my hon. friend from Macdonald (Mr. Boyd) that I think he is a little in error when he says that the gentleman who was then brought here as an expert and later on appointed as chief inspector of weights and measures; was half a blacksmith and half a scale manufacturer. Mr. Fyfe is well known throughout the Dominion as one ofl the best qualified men that we could find. Hff was strongly recommended not only by the scale manufacturers in the Dominion, but by many other people who had had the advantage of ascertaining his qualifications. I may say that in many instances I am told that large corporations, such as the Grand Trunk Railway and Canadian Pacific Railway companies, have invited Mr. Fyfe to act as their expert. After having examined the weighing machine in the presence of Mr. Magness he said that the machine was not in compliance with the law, and at that time Mr. Magness seemed to admit that it was true. I wish to state here that my hou. friend is again in error when he says that it was very easy for the department to change the law and admit to verification that weighing machine. I know he is not a lawyer, but he might have asked some lawyer, who might have told him that it was impossible for the department to change the law by Order in Council. That section was read and properly interpreted yesterday by my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Roche).

speechtext:
Yes, I will answer my hon. friend in a moment or two. I have not now, what I expect to have, three or four cases in which, for certain purposes, weighing machines were admitted to verification because they were in conformity with the law. That is my information, but I will be in a position in a

few minutes, or later on, to give instances and show cases as they actually are. When that question was brought before the House last year I stated that Mr. Magness would be in a position later on to supply the market with a good weighing machine complying ill every respect with the law. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Boyd) cannot expect that the head of the department or any officer .of the department could of their own knowledge decide whether a machine should be admitted to verification or not. As to that we have to accept the decision of the chief inspector and I am glad to say that he has always spoken with authority. I have no doubt that my hon. friend (Mr. Boyd) and my hon. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) have faithfully represented the views of the farmers of the North-west and of Manitoba, and I believe myself that the difficulties of litigation with regard to the threshing of grain must be remedied as soon as possible. But I ask my hon. friend, if the position of the owners of the threshing machines and the farmers would be any better even if we had admitted to verification a machine which did not comply with the law. Had we done that, it would have increased the litigation because any body who had anything to do with a contract might go before the court and say to the owner of that thrashing machine :	I will not pay
because that machine is not in conformity with the law. Neither would the certificate be sufficient in such a ease, because X know of one or! two instances in which decisions have been rendered in the courts of the province of Quebec where the certificate was held not to be sufficient. The department has not been negligent in trying to secure a machine which would give satisfaction and at the same time put a stop to litigation. I understood my hon. friend (Mr. Boyd), to say yesterday, that the farmers and the owners of these machines had to use certain vessels pending the advent of a machine which would give satisfaction, but if they had been provided with a machine which did not comply with the law I imagine that the difficulties would have been the same. If the weighing machine was not a legal one, even though it had been approved and a certificate given, another litigation would have followed. I will not touch for the present at least on the political part of the speech of my hon. friend from Macdonald (Mr. Boyd). I am ready and the department is ready to give to the farmers of the North-west a machine which will be satisfactory, but hon. gentlemen will hardly contend that the department is bound to invent a machine. That must be left to the ingenuity of the individual, and at least credit must be given to the department for having in its service, Mr. Magness who has done his best to meet the wants of the people of the North-west. When Mr. Magness was here, and after he had Hon. Mr. BERNIER.
talked with Mr. Fife, he made up his mind to make some changes which had been suggested to him by Mr. Fyfe. X presume that this has been done, and if my information is correct, a machine will be supplied to the farmers of Manitoba and the North-west for next season. Inquiries have been made by the department in several countries where such machines are in vogue, and if it is found impossible to get a machine which will comply with the terms of the law, then with the assent of my friends on both sides of the House, I will bring in a measure in order to relieve the just grievances of these people.

The hon. gentleman has not been able to tell us how much longer than a year it has continued because lie only dates his information from the date when he assumed control of the department. Does the hon. minister really think that it is the people of Manitoba and the North-west Territories should be obliged, in order to carry on their business effectively, to violate the law ? Does he think that a year or more is a. reasonable time to allow that condition to continue. I am inclined to think that some greater activity than has been manifested by the hon. gentleman in the past should be manifested in the future; that he should bestir himself a little more about this matter and bring the existing condition of things to a very speedy conclusion. It is greatly to be regretted that the condition should have ever been created at all. but having once been created it is certainly most desirable that every means should be taken to bring it to a conclusion as soon as possible.

Mr. JOHN CHARLTON (North Norfolk) moved second reading of Bill (No. 3) to amend the Dominion Elections Act, 1900. Pie said : Mr. Speaker, in moving the second reading of this Bill, I may perhaps be permitted to make a few observations bearing upon what I conceive to be the necessity for some enlarged scope of the Elections Act as regards offences, and increased stringency ns regards punishments. The necessity for preserving the purity of the electorate lies at the very foundation of the maintenance of the perpetuity of free institutions. A pure, patriotic electorate will ensure to a country the continuance of free institutions and good government. A celebrated American poet has said :
The crowning fact, the kingliest act Of freedom is a free man's vote.
He does not refer to the man that keeps that article for sale; he does not refer to the venal vote, the purchasable vote; but he refers to the vote of the man who esteems his franchise a priceless heritage, and will exercise it according to his convictions and beliefs relating to public policy and the conduct of public affairs.
The necessity for the maintenance of this condition of things is one the importance
of which we cannot overestimate. In this country there are being laid the foundations of a nation-a nation which may hope to attain great prominence in the affairs of the world in the future; a nation which may hope to have an enormous population, great resources, great wealth, and a first-class influence among the nations of the world. But our hopes as to the future can hardly be realized if we permit the virus of corruption to infect the blood of the people. If we permit this, we shall simply have entailed upon us the consequences that have invariably followed political corruption and the debasing of the electorate.
The expression is frequently used; we are devoted to measures, not men. But measures cannot be carried into operation without men. We must have men who are the incarnation of good government and good measures in order to carry these measures into effect; and we can hardly have that class of men under a condition of things where the vote of a country is purchasable. If an electorate is for sale, if it is a question of the amount of money expended as to who shall be elected as its representative, then the very foundations of the stability of our institutions are swept away. The man who so far forgets his duty as a citizen as to purchase his election by a lavish expenditure of money, is a man who is likely to take measures to recoup himself for the expense which he has incurred; and the electorate which has chosen such it man ns its representative has no right to expect any other line of conduct.
Our future depends, I have said, on the purity of the electorate; and if the system of corrupting the electorate cannot be stamped out, of course the evil will grow rapidly in magnitude. If the lavish expenditure' of money is to be a necessary feature of running an electoral contest, then it becomes a matter of primary importance to political parties to provide funds for election purposes, and there is an inevitable tendency to corrupt practices on the part of the government in power. We had an instance of this in 1872, when the government in power felt the necessity of securing a large sum of money for the approaching election contests of that year; and the method adopted by that government, the sale of a great public charter, was one of a most demoralizing character, which became a permanent blot on the history of this country. The influences which led to that violation of the proper rules of public conduct will be at work now and at all times in the future if we have a purchasable electorate and are unable to stamp out this evil; and these influences will naturally lead to actions on the part of governments that cannot be condoned or excused-the scaling of subsidies, rake-offs, methods which politicians do not need to be instructed in or to have alluded to: there will be a powerful incentive that will lead governments to resort to these means to ob-

tain money. In order to secure purity of administration, we must have purity in the electorate; and in order to have purity in the electorate, we must adopt means absolutely to stamp out the influences and the evils that are growing in magnitude in this country day by day.
As to the extent of electoral corruption, I do not know how great it may be. As to whether it is a crime to increase this extent of electoral corruption, I have no doubt whatever. It is a crime of the first magnitude, and a crime that we ought to adopt methods, so far as we possibly can, to avoid. As to the extent of electoral corruption, I say I do not know how great it may be. I suppose I need not attempt to instruct any member of this House with regard to that matter. I dare say we are all well aware that it is an evil of considerable extent, if not of great extent, in this Dominion. I presume we are all aware that very many ridings are influenced in the elections by the corrupt expenditure of money-that there are ridings where the result of the election is merely a matter of how much money is spent, and which party will spend the most. There are ridings which ought to be disfranchised owing to the thorough, absolute corruption of the electorate. As to which of our political parties is the worst, naturally the Conservatives will say that the bulk of this work is done by the other side and naturally the Reformers will take the opposite view ; but I think it will be found that one is just as bad as the other. Each one spends all the money it can. Instead of vieing with each other in these corrupt practices, we had better vie in the attempt to put them down. If we study the question over we can find the means of doing so and thus confer untold blessings upon the country. At present the candidate who prosecutes his canvass on proper lines, who avoids the improper expenditure of money, is, in nine cases out of ten, heavily handicapped. He is clogged in the race and many a man who would refrain from this kind of work, is compelled to do it in order to meet similar influences which are working against him. Elections can scarcely be run under present conditions without the expenditure of money. What should be the object of our law governing elections ? Its primary object should be to put an end to these practices by adopting measures that cannot fail to do so. We should not hesitate to apply drastic remedies. We should increase the number of offences and the severity of sentences and punishments, and if we do so to a sufficient extent I believe we will succeed in stamping out the practices. So far as electoral corruption is concerned, I am informed that in most of the states of the American union it has been absolutely stamped out. That has been the case in the states of New York and Pennsylvania. Three weeks ago there was a trial in the city of Buffalo concerning the

election of a sheriff. The sheriff was charged with having promised an office and some emoluments to a friend for his assistance in the election. He was liable, on conviction, to be sentenced to five years in the penitentiary, but escaped on a verdict of ' not proven.' The law of that state is now in such shape that it is perilous to indulge in any of these illicit practices. The man who pays a bribe puts himself at the mercy of the seallawag who takes the money. This is so perilous that the practice has ceased. I believe that we can reach the same result here. The present law does not go far enough, and I propose some amendments which will have the effect of giving it the requisite extension. Perhaps tile promoters of that law intended it to go as far as necessary. But it has not put an end to corruption. On the contrary, corruption is spreading rapidly and the influence of this condition of things shows itself in other lines of public life. The best elements of the country are alarmed. Men of all parties deplore this condition of things and ask whether there is not some remedy. Can we not put an end to this evil which threatens the well-being and stability of our state. The amendment I am about to submit creates in the first place a few more offences. In that respect the original Act is not ns comprehensive as it should be. It also increases the penalties to such an extent that infractions of the law, if the accused be convicted, involve not only a loss of money but loss of liberty. These are penalties which will make crime odious and cause every man to shrink from the consequences.
Without further general remarks let me call the attention of the House to the provisions of this Bill. Section 108, law 1900, relating to Dominion elections gives a number of offences in detail, as set out in subsection ' A ' to ' I.' I propose to add three more subsections, ' J,' ' K ' and ' L.' Subsection ' J ' is as follows :-
(j.) Every person who by abduction, duress or any forcible or fraudulent device or contrivance, impedes, prevents or otherwise interferes with the free exercise of the elective franchise by any voter, or compels, induces, or prevails upon any voter to give or refrain from giving his vote for or against any candidate at any election ;
Subsection ' IC ' is as follows :-
(k.) Every person who, being an employer, pays his employees the wages or salary due, in pay envelopes, upon which there is written or printed any political motto, device or argument containing threats, express or implied, intended or calculated to influence the political opinions or actions of such employees, or within ninety days of a general election puts or otherwise exhibits in the establishment or place where his employees are engaged in labour, any handbill or placard containing any threat, notice or information, that if any particular ticket or candidate is elected or defeated, work in his place or establishment will cease in whole or

in part, his establishment will be closed up, or the wages of his employees will be reduced, or other threats, express or implied, intended or calculated to influence the political opinions or actions of his employees ;
The following is subsection ' L ':-
(1.) Every person who, being an officer or employee of Canada or of any province thereof, directly or indirectly uses his authority or official influence to compel or induce any other such officer or employee to pay or promise to pay any political assessment, or-
(2.) Being an officer or employee of Canada or any province thereof, directly or indirectly gives, pays or hands over to any officer such officer or employee, any money or other valuable thing on account of, or to be applied to, the promotion of his election, appointment or retention in office, or makes any promise or gives any subscription to such officer or employee to pay or contribute any money or other valuable thing for such purpose or object,-or
(3.) Prepares or makes out or takes any part in preparing or making out any political assessment, subscription or contribution, or sends or presents any political assessment, subscription or contribution to, or requests its payment of, any such officer or employee;
These are the three subsections which I propose to add to section 108 of tlie law of 1900, and I propose to change the character of the punishment as follows :-
And every person so offending

that is, committing any of the offences in this alphabetical list from ' A ' to ' L '-

is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years, and shall forfeit a sum not exceeding five hundred dollars to any person who sues therefor, with costs, and shall be disfranchised for a period of seven years, or, in case the offence is committed by a corporation, it shall forfeit its charter.
Provided always, that the actual personal expenses of any candidate, his expenses for actual professional services performed, and bona fide payments for the fair cost of printing, advertising, bill posting and rent of halls or rooms for meetings, shall be held to be expenses lawfully incurred, and the payment thereof shall not be a violation of this Act.
The following section I have copied from the Penal Code of the State of New York, and upon it I would rely more than upon any other provision of the Bill for putting an end to the evils I am speaking of. This would be substituted for sections 134, 135, and 136. It would be a section general in its character, more comprehensive, more easily understood, terser and more epi-gramatical. It is to be inserted after section 108, and would be numbered 108a :
A person offending against any provision of the next preceding section of this Act

-that is, against any of subsections ' A ' to ' Ij ' of section 108-
-is a competent witness against another person so offending, and may be compelled to attend and testify on any trial, hearing, proceeding, or investigation in the same manner as any other person. The testimony so given shall not be used in any prosecution or proceeding civil or criminal against the person testifying. A person testifying shall not therefor be liable to indictment, prosecution or punishment for the offence with reference to which his testimony was given, and may plead or prove the giving of testimony accordingly, in bar of such indictment or prosecution.
Now, under this section, the man who is bribed may bring an action against the briber, and the penalty is $500, or less at the discretion of the court, payable to the complainant, and any number of men who have been bribed may be subpoenaed as witness and may give their testimony under the provision of this Act which exonerates them from all consequences, civil or criminal in relation to this matter. It is found that, in the state of New York, under the provisions of this Act, the business of bribing men to vote-a business which is carried on with a certain degree of impunity under our laws-is one in which the consequences are so grave, the Act so perilous, the briber being so completely at the mercy of the parties who take his bribe, that parties conclude not to go into it. So the money is not forthcoming and the agents are not there to distribute it. In fact, the business cannot be carried on with safety, and there is an end to the whole thing. We have to adopt something of this kind if we are to cope with this evil in Canada. And if this section 108a is put in our law, it will absolutely put a quietus on the whole business of buying electors at the polls. The fine going to the informant, it will be an inducement to him to bring the briber to book. The briber will be so completely at the mercy of the bribed that there will be an end of the whole business.
4.	Section number 126 of the said Act is repealed, and the following is substituted therefor :-
126. Any person who, while a candidate for the House of Commons either before or after nomination day, is guilty of bribery, fraud, or wilful violation of any election law, shall be for ever disqualified from holding an office of trust or profit under the government of Canada, and shall be disfranchised for the period of seven years next after his being so found guilty.
This is copied from the Penal Code of the state of Pennsylvania, and renders any candidate who is guilty of bribery or fraud ineligible for office for life.
5.	Section 142 of the said Act is amended by substituting the words ' seven years ' for the words ' one year ' in the fifth line thereof.
The provisions of this Act will necessarily require consideration and argument in Committee. I shall not detain the House longer with arguments on the Bill the general feature of which I have attempted to put before the House. I beg to move the second reading of this Bill.

Mr. Speaker, I had no intention of taking up the time of the House discussing questions of political morality, but it does seem to me that the lecture which we have just received comes with very bad grace from the lips of an hon. gentleman who invaded the riding of South Ontario to call upon the Conservatives great and Conservatives small to rally round the standard of that self-convicted criminal, Mr. Billy Smith, after he had made the scandalous revelations in the witness box which he did make.
I wish to say in answer to the hon. member for South Essex (Mr. Cowan) that he makes a statement he is not warranted in making. Mr. William Smith never was a convicted criminal.
A self-confessed criminal.
Let me say that Mr. Smith was a respectable member of the community when I went to his convention.
And asked them to nominate him.

Mr. Speaker, as a personal friend of Mr. Wm. Smith, I would not be doing my duty were I not to resent publicly, and in the most emphatic way I can, what has been said here to-day by the hon. member for South Essex (Mr. Cowan). I can tell the hon. member for South Essex, say what he will about Mr. Smith, that Mr. Smith stands to-day in the hearts of the people of South Ontario, irrespective of politics, as an honest and truthful man, at all events. Now, what was the position ? There was a keen contest being waged in the riding of South Ontario, on the Conservative side by Mr. Charles Calder, and on the Liberal side by Mr. John Dry-den. I am not going to say here what has prevailed in elections in South Ontario, as conducted by Mr. John Dryden ; the courts prove that, they prove it distinctly and they prove beyond contradiction that Mr. John Dryden has never dared to face a court in Ontario or a judicial decision, because, when brought to bay, he has thrown up the sponge and confessed bribery wholesale throughout the whole riding. What was the position of Mr. Smith ? Mr. Smith, knowing that there was only one way of fighting fire, and that is with fire, on his own behalf, and with other independent men in the riding, irrespective of Mr. Caider, went to work to fight Mr. Dryden in South Ontario in the then ensuing elections. What was the result ? A fund was subscribed, and that fund is placed in Mr. Smith's hands. When Mr. Smith went upon the witness stand, with the fear of God on the one side, he told the truth of it, and what was the answer afterwards ? What was the answer,
I ask the hon. member for South Essex ? Mr. Smith was a candidate in that riding during the last election, and he polled within seventy votes of the number polled by the hon. member (Mr. Ross, Ontario) who represents that riding, and when it is considered that Mr. Smith has always had narrow majorities in South Ontario, when it is considered that on that occasion a dead set was made against him in the riding, that the force of the McLaughlin Carriage Company, which in former elections had been almost passive in Oshawa, was on that occasion thrown against him, it is no matter of wonderment that Mr. Smith was defeated. In prior elections, owing to the fact that the McLaughlin Carriage Company had given a quiet support indirectly to Mr. Smith ; at least, it had not interfered against Mr. Smith, he was elected by narrow majorities, but owing to the fact that this Liberal government had protected the McLaughlin Bros, to a greater extent than ever before,

McLaughlin Bros., with the men they command in the riding and with the other forces they control, went against Mr. Smith in the campaign, and the result was that Mr. Smith lost the election. I am not going to say that there were any improper means taken on behalf of the hon. member who represents that riding, but I believe that hon. gentleman will say that as far as Mr. Smith and his friends are concerned in the last campaign no improper or illegal means were resorted to on his behalf. Here was the position : Mr. Smith had made this honest confession under oath that there was a fund. Mr. Dryden had gone into the witness box and with sanctimonious mien had made out that he knew nothing of the means resorted to to secure his election against Mr. Calder on that occasion. Who were the men who brought about the election of Mr. Dryden ? Why, Sir, there was not a party hack from one end of the province to the other that was not in the riding. The Sullivan gang, who stand to-day hitched up with the Provincial Secretary, were on every highway and side line in South Ontario. I can recall the names of dozens of men brought into the riding, and here was Mr. Smith and the local workers putting up their hard earned money and fighting against this gang brought in there from outside. I have known Mr. Smith since I first came to this House eleven or twelve years ago ; I have known Mr. Smith as prominent in stockraising in Ontario, and let me tell hon. gentlemen in this House that, in the business in which he is concerned, as a stock importer, Mr. Smith occupies one of the most prominent positions in this province, and any man who knows Mr. Smith knows that he is a man of sterling worth, a man of great honesty and one, who, when it came to a question of political preferment or of telling the truth, sank political preferment in preference to telling what was untrue. Mr. Smith is the darling idol of the Conservatives of South Ontario. Why should he not be ? He is a gallant and courageous fighter when up against odds, and after the fight, when it came to a question of truthfulness and honour, he was prepared to tell the truth even to the great hurt of himself and of his friends. Once again I resent the imputation cast upon Mr. Smith, and I beg to say that Liberals as well as Conservatives in their heart of hearts have more respect for Mr. Smith than for John Dryden in the riding of South Ontario.

I am very glad that the hon. member for South Essex (Mr. Cowan) has brought the matter before this House. I know it has been heralded broadcast throughout the country that Mr. Smith is a criminal. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Cowan) being a lawyer, I would like to have his assistance in getting the administration of justice to straighten out this tangle. The administration of justice

throughout Canada is controlled by the Liberal government from Ottawa, and the Liberal government in Ontario have control of the administration of justice in that province. Now, if William Smith is a criminal, how can the hon. gentleman (Mr. Cowan) charge the Conservative party of Canada with negligence of duty in not prosecuting that criminal ?
Does the hon. gentleman want an answer now ?
I will take my seat if you wish to speak.

The reason why is expressed in the following statement of Judge Ferguson
I have some regret that this large offender Mr. Smith is not before us. X have nothing to say of him but that his evidence is the most glaring piece of corruption that I have ever heard.
The reason Mr. Smith was not before them was because they could not get him before them, however anxious they might be on account of the statute of limitations standing in the way.

Do I understand the hon. gentleman (Mr. Cowan) to say that Wm. Smith left the province in order to evade justice ? Mr. Smith resides in South Ontario and he has resided there ever since continually, and he gave this evidence himself.
The court did not believe him.
I understand tiiat the court believed him and condemned him on his own evidence.

Will my hon. friend pardon me.
Some hon. MUMBERS. Order. Don't interrupt.

I know that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Ingram) wants to be fair even if some gentlemen on the other side do not. This is the statement of Judge Osier :
I should not call Mr. Smith's^manner candid. He showed a disposition to "fence with the counsel. I should call it brazen, that is the word. I look upon the evidence cf Smith as being a brazen, distinct, strong denial ; a denial that I do not believe.

I rose with the intention of being fair and I hope to have the hearing of at least gentlemen in this House who desire to he fair. If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Cowan) will carefully read the evidence in the South Ontario case he will find that Mr. Smith admitted having expending something like $1,200 during that election.
Certainly.
That he collected a fund for that purpose and expended it.
Not collected ; but he said he spent it.
He admitted in court that he handled the fund, and that was the evidence. Now, if Mr. Smith has done wrong and is a criminal, why is it I ask that the Department of Justice has not prosecuted him ?

At the time the prosecution took place there had been no charge made against Wm. Smith, because the evidence was not brought out until the trial. They did not have him before them, and the statute of limitations then steps in
Did not the judges have the power to imprison him ?
No.
Yes.

I leave it to my hon. friend and the lawyers on this side of the House to settle that. But this much I do know, and it is that the Department of Justice has been lax in prosecuting offenders under the Election law. It does not lie in the mouth of any person to charge the Conservatives with not prosecuting that class of criminal. Let me say that Mr. Smith lias been a highly respected member of this House. He had as good a record as perhaps any other member in this House during the time he was here, and more than that, I will say that Wm. Smith is not the only person in this country who could give evidence of that kind if they chose to be honest. It is notorious that those who administer justice in the province of Ontario have little to their credit for the manner in which they have administered the law against electoral corruption. * In the county of Elgin to my knowledge, they have allowed criminals time and again to leave that county and go unwhipt of justice.
Will the hon. gentleman permit me to ask a question.
Yes.

I do not desire to bring out these post mortems, but the hon. gentleman must know that in the West Elgin case, when the warrant was issued against Pritchett, that warrant was got out of the possession of the constable, so Pritchett stated, by one of the hon. members now representing the city of Hamilton, and by Mr. O. E. Fleming, of Windsor, and that it was impossible for them to issue a second warrant upon that information and therefore the absence of a warrant allowed the fugitive to escape.

Mr. Pritchett resided in the city of London and the Liberal government dare not prosecute him. He had nothing to fear from the Liberal party. They dare not prosecute him. What else could he. do but make his peace with the



Conservative party in order to come back to this country. He liad no fear of the Liberal party at all. The hon. member for Hamilton is here to speak for himself. We know perfectly well that this Pritchett was iii South Ontario and that Thomas Lewis was there to, and to-day Lewis administers the license law-3 of the province of Ontario in the department of Mr. Stratton.

I did not catch exactly the expression used by the hon. member for South Essex (Mr. Cowan), but I understand he quotes somebody as saying, that the member for Hamilton on some occasion got a warrant against the man Pritchett out of some one's possession and so prevented his prosecution. I do not know who said that, but it is an absolute falsehood.
Hear, hear.
And any man who says it or pretends to assert that it is a fact, tells an absolute falsehood, Mr. Speaker.

Hear, hear.
Mr. COWAN I know that Pritchett swore to it on his oath and the hon. gentleman (Mr. Barker) has not so far as I know ever denied it before.

It is somewhat unusual I think to make an attack of this character upon a gentleman who is not in the House, for the purpose of attempting to discredit an hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) who made a speech which certainly was not of a partisan character. However, I have heard my hon. friend from South Essex (Mr. Cowan) pursue tactics of that kind before and I cannot say that X was very much surprised at it to-day. If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Cowan) would look around, possibly he might find in the ranks of the Liberal party to-day gentlemen who had experienced the result of a trial in the election court. I do not propose to follow his methods and to make references that I could make if I desired to pursue the tactics of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Cowan). I would just suggest to him that possibly in the future some of his own friends would thank him, if he did not introduce matters of this kind; otherwise some references which might not be very pleasant will perhaps be made. My hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Rt. Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) has enunciated his views in regard to matters of this kind. Some eleven years ago he spoke with reference to these things, and I happen to have in my hand the expression of that right hon. gentleman's views with regard to one constituency in Canada. He said :
He knew there was a large number of men in the country who wanted to be bought. He knew that because he had bought them twice when he was an unrepentant sinner.

I commend that expression of opinion to my hon. friend from South Essex (Mr. Cowan).
I will also ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce to thank the member for South Essex for another quotation which I shall make. The right hon. gentleman (Rt. Hon. , Sir Richard Cartwright) said, this in the House of Commons :
I am speaking a most lamentable, but at the same time a most certain truth when I say that as regards the 215 constituencies of this Dominion with the exception of a very small percentage, the balance of power under our system is practically placed in the hands of the most corrupt section of the community. I make this statement advisedly as I make it with very great regret, but it is so and to all intents and purposes the only practical difficulty which stands in the way of the party possessing the reins of power, and having at their disposal sufficient sums of money, is simply the difficulty of bringing these corrupt means into direct anl actual contact with the great masses of the electors. Were that mechanical difficulty, as I might almost call it, overcome then I have no doubt whatever that the opposition in this country would be practically exterminated at any general election that might take place.
We have seen some of the efforts that have been made within the last few years to overcome this mechanical difficulty. We have seen gangs of men, outsiders, hired for the purpose, going into many constituencies for the purpose of overcoming the mechanical difficulty referred to by the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce. No one who has weighed the evidence can have any doubt that the Hon. Peter White was elected at the by-election at Brockville, and there is equally little doubt that the Conservative candidate was elected at the by election in West Huron. Both of these elections were stolen, and the government accepted the stolen goods ; and after the election courts revealed certain facts, the government, or the followers of the government at least, used every effort in their power to prevent an investigation notwithstanding certain promises which were made in this House ; and when the motion to continue the investigation was made in this House at the following session, it was voted down, and there has been no investigation since, and Mr. Pritchett, the man who worked these elections, has not been prosecuted. After leaving the country, he came back and openly stated that he knew he would not be prosecuted, because the Liberal government dare not prosecute him, and he has continued to remain here, and the government not dared to prosecute him. I did not intend to bring these matters before the House at the present time ; but when we see such tactics as those adopted by the hon. member for South Essex (Mr. Cowan) to-day. hon. gentlemen opposite will not take it amiss, I suppose. If I call to their attention certain matters-and the list is by no means exhausted-which have somewhat affected their status in days gone by.

So far as the merits of the Bill are concerned, I would not like to commit myself at present to every word or line of it; hut certainly it is one which should go to a second reading and which should result in useful legislation. There is no doubt that means are employed in elections in this country which are altogether opposed not only to the spirit but the letter of the law. I am not speaking from a partisan standpoint; I am speaking of facts which we all know to exist, and while the law may quite properly be amended in the direction my hon. friend has suggested, I think the chief difliculty at the present time is that there are no sufficient means provided for enforcing the law. I am not sure that it may not be the duty of this government or of some subsequent government to make some provision for an officer who would have the same independence as the Auditor General, and whose duty it would be to look into any election in Canada where there is suspicion of any corruption, and to act as a public prosecutor, to see that those guilty of corruption and wrong-doing should be brought to Justice. Another suggestion has been made, which I think deserves the attention of the government as well as of us who are sitting in opposition; I mean the suggestion that one possible remedy for bribery at elections might be found in the enactment of a law providing that any man failing to vote at an election without sufficient excuse should lose the right to vote for a certain period afterwards, say seven years. At present there are two great abuses with regard to men voting at elections. One is the practice of paying men to stay at home and not vote. That is a sure way of making the use of money effective. In that way you cut down the vote of the opposite side. Then, there is the corrupt man who stays at home and will not go to the polls at all unless he is paid. I for one would be inclined to give a measure containing the amendments I have suggested very careful and favourable consideration.
Mr. EDWARD IIACKETT (West Prince, P.E.I.) Mr. Speaker, the Bill of the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) meets with my full approval and support; but I would like to have added to it a clause that would compel the returning officer, in case of a recount, to deliver the ballot boxes to the judge of the county court. I have had experience of this need. We have been discussing to-day matters concerning the province of Ontario. I was elected at the last general election by a majority of three, and was declared elected. My opponent asked for a recount, and the ballot boxes were ordered to be taken from Alberton, in West Prince, to Summerside, where the judge resides. What happened in the meantime ? During their transit between Alberton and Summerside, one of the ballot boxes, in which I had a majority of thirty-five votes, was stolen from the car, for the pur-29*
pose of preventing the ballots being counted and depriving me of the seat I hold in this parliament. It makes very little difference whether Smith, Jones, Brown or Robinson holds the seat; but it is important that the electors of Canada should be protected, not only in casting their votes on the day of election, but in having their votes placed in the custody of the proper authorities. I brought this matter up in this parliament in the session of 1901, and explained the facts. I said then, as I say now, that the Minister of Railways, (Hon. Mr. Blair) was responsible for the safe delivery of those ballot boxes by the conductors and brakesmen in charge of the railway. These men are held responsible for the safe delivery of a barrel of flour or a barrel of sugar; yet they allowed the votes of a number of people in West Prince to be lost without making any effort to ascertain what had become of them. When the gentlemen who occupy the treasury benches saw that a hundred people in a polling division were being deprived of their rights and privileges as voters, why did they not make an effort to ascertain what had become of that ballot box ? But nothing was done. They allowed the transaction to pass without comment or action, simply because it was intended to deprive your humble servant of his place in this parliament.

I would like to add a clause to this Bill, if the mover has no objection :
That any person found guilty of subscribing money towards an election fund with a view of bribing the electorate, shall be subject to a fine of not less than $500 and liable to six months' imprisonment.

Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time, and House went into Committee thereon.
On section 1.

Take this subsection
(k) which reads :-
(k) Every person who, being an employer, pays his employees the wages or salary due, in pay envelopes, upon which there is written or printed any political motto, device or argument containing threats, express or implied, intended or calculated to influence the political opinions or actions of such employees, or within ninety days of a general election puts or otherwise exhibits in the establishment or place where his employees are engaged in labour, any handbill or placard containing any threat, notice or information, that if any particular ticket or candidate is elected or defeated, work in his place or establishment will cease in whole or in part, his establishment will be closed up, or the wages of his employees will be reduced, or other threats, express or implied, intended or calculated to influence the political opinions or actions of his employees.
It seems to me that if the hon. member for Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) will go back a few years, he will recollect when the great party to which he belongs had, as part of

its stock in trade in the election campaign, a certain pictorial exhibit which would come under this clause. Or if he does not, the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Rt. Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) may recall that in the elections of 1891, his party made considerable capital out of a picture entitled ' putting the mortgage on the farm.' The artist depicted in that picture the worn out physiognomy of the wife, the sickly faces of the children, the pale features and tottering hand of the farmer as he was about putting his signature to the mortgage, and then the lesson was conveyed that unless the protective tariff were abolished in its entirety, foreclosure would inevitably follow. Surely the hon. member for North Norfolk is not going to prevent his party leader from putting before the public gaze once more pictures that may illustrate the effects of its policy. The particular picture to which 1 have referred may not be produced but there may be others. There may be pictures showing the prosperity of these manufacturers who have been given increased protection by this government. Now that the agricultural implements interest in this Dominion has been placed in a solid position by having two senators engaged in that business to represent it in the Upper Chamber, surely the hon. gentleman will not take from these two gentlemen the right to display illustrations in their establishments, showing how well the present tariff has worked in their interests. Surely he will not prevent the carriage manufacturers, who are benefited by a ttve per cent increased duty on cutters, depicting to an interested public the good effects of this increased protection given by the present government. I would ask the hon. gentleman to think over that clause, and perhaps out of gratitude to that old picture of the mortgage on the farm he may revise his opinion.

* The hon. gentleman lias made a comparison which does not apply. I am not professing in this clause to deal with the legitimate methods of influencing public opinion. It is a legitimate method to publish articles in newspapers and pictures in newspapers and to disseminate information in a general way. This clause does not seek to interfere with the liberty of the subject in that effect. Its object is to prevent personal threats by the employers. It deals only with an improper exercise of influence by an employer over his employees. It deals with the attempt to intimidate them by threats, to influence their action, by threatening to deprive them of employment or reduce their wages- actions just as reprehensible as the purchase of votes or the purchase of electors to remain away from the poll, actions which the law condemns and which are quite distinct from attempts made in a general way. by arguments on the platform or through

the press or by pictorial illustrations for general circulation, to produce an impression on the general public. This subsection is to prohibit an employer from approaching an employee with threats to deprive him of employment or reduce his wages.

If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Charlton) will permit me, I would like to ask him a question. Suppose that the employer of labour, instead of making these threats himself causes some one to circulate a report that the loss of employment or reduction of wages will follow the giving of voting in a certain way. This would be quite as effective as a direct threat. How does the hon. gentleman meet that ?
Under the provisions of the law, that would be an improper influence.
It is not specified, and it might be a very difficult thing to trace. If the employer were charged with it he might say that it was merely a general rumour for which he was not responsible.
What bearing has that upon this subsection ?

The hon. gentleman is attempting to remedy an evil, but there would be no remedy if the employer did not, personally commit the offence-and, of course, he would take good care not to identify himself with such a threat, but would take equally good care that somebody else should make that threat for him. I would like to call attention also to this clause :
(j.) Every person who by abduction, duress or any forcible or fraudulent device or contrivance, impedes, prevents or otherwise interferes with the free exercise of the elective franchise by any voter, or compels, induces, or prevails upon any voter to give or refrain from giving his vote for or against any candidate at any election ;	.
Now, the hon. gentleman had in his mind the repeal of section 112, because this would be a portion of section 112. There are many other means of intimidation that could not come under the provisions of this Bill. I have a Bill myself on the same subject. In the province of Ontario, the hon. gentleman knows very well, there is no secret ballot. And he knows very well also that that fact is made use of at every local election in the province of Ontario- not openly, it is true, because then it would lose its effect-to intimidate the electors, and that electors are so intimidated from one end of the province to the other. Men are told that they need not hope tol escape punishment if they vote against certain candidates, or, at least, that their only hope Is in the mercy of the men who know just how they vote. I have a Bill providing that every person who declares that the Dominion'ballot, which, as a matter of fact in a secret ballot, is not secret, shall be

punished. Men who have told that the local ballot is not secret, and have no means of knowing whether it is or not, hare been intimidated on more than one occasion by the statement that the Dominion ballot likewise is not secret. I have a Bill making it an indictable offence for any one to make that statement to intimidate voters. If you repeal section 112, which enumerates many actions which are offences under the law, you make it impossible to punish persons guilty of those actions. I am not a lawyer, but I venture to state that no lawyer drew the hon. gentleman's (Mr. Charlton's) Bill. It was drawn by a layman, I am sure, and it is quite as faulty as one would be that I might draw myself. I hope the hon. gentleman will not insist upon the form of his measure. And I am going to appeal to the Minister of Justice (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick) upon this point. I would suggest to that hon. gentleman that we should not consider his Bill without considering also the Bill that I have on the same subject. I do not know anything that would be more likely to open the door to the very evils that, I have do doubt, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Charlton) means to remedy than the changes lie proposes-without considering the general effect of those changes. The hon. gentleman simply adopts a part of seetioh 112 and repeals the rest of that section. I am sure the Minister of Justice will agree with me. And I would ask him, for he is a good lawyer, not to attempt to deal with this Bill without considering other Bills on the subject. I think we should not have gone into Committee on this Bill without having at least taken into consideration, other Bills the enactment of which might be prevented by passing this one.
I think the hon. gentleman's (Mr. Charlton's) Bill is in the right direction. But I do not know whether it is intended to refer to companies employing labour.
It is.
It seems to me that it is for individuals rather than for companies.
It applies to companies also, and the penalty for violation is that the company loses its charter.

I would like to quote an instance involving a point which this Bill should be made to cover. In the last provincial election in North Perth, a certain railway official used his influence on behalf of a certain candidate. When remonstrated with, he denied using his influence, and to square himself he issued a circular something like this:	'This is to certify that
every employee of the company is at liberty to vote for John Brown without interference.' Now, John Brown happened to be the Liberal candidate. So, the employees
were told that they were at liberty to vote for the Liberal candidate. We should have a section of the Election Act providing that any interference on the part of a superintendent or general manager or other official of a railway designed to influence the votes of employees of the company should be a violation of the law. This would be a section in the interests of all, for we must realize that managers of these institutions are not always Liberals, and that the Liberal government will not always have it in their power to use influence with the employees of railway companies or other large corporations.

I would like to read to the hon. Minister of Justice (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick) the provision of Bill (No. 15) and to ask him to say whether it is covered by the Bill we are now discussing :
1. Section 112 of the Dominion Elections Act, 1900, is amended by adding after the word ' loss ' in the fifth line thereof, the following words: ' or makes use of any language to the effect that the ballot to he used or the mode of voting at the election is not secret.'
I ask the hon. gentleman now if section j of section 1, in the Bill of the hon. member for North Norfolk would include an offence such as I propose to punish in my Bill ?

I have carefully considered the hon. gentleman's Bill, and my impression is that his suggested amendment would be absolutely useless to effect the object he aims at. It would be useless, because his object is to reach the process of intimidation and to stop it. It is intimidation to say to a man : If you vote in this particular way I shall know it; I will know how you vote, because the ballot is not secret, and by the knowledge I have acquired, by the fact that the ballot is not secret, I will be able to injure you. There is a process of intimidation. Now section 112 says :
Every one who, directly or indirectly, by himself or by any other person on his behalf, makes use of, or threatens to make use of, any force, violence or restraint, or inflicts, or threatens the infliction, by himself, or by or through any other person, of any injury, damage, harm or loss

Then the section goes on to say :
-or in any manner practices intimidation.
Now these general words are broad enough to cover the case suggested by my bon. friend, and it seems to me meets, as far as possible, the case he suggests. I think in drafting legislation of this sort it is always wise to make the words general enough to cover every case, instead of specializing a case, as suggested by his amendment.

The hon. gentleman will permit me to say that I have stopped fai'

short of what he has read, and say ' any manner of intimidation.'

I hardly think, with all due deference to the opinion of the Minister of Justice, that the case comes within the term * intimidation.' A voter might not like to have his manner of voting known, and yet might not be oppressed by any sense of fear, he might not desire to have it known for social or business reasons. The fact would remain, however, that he did not desire it to be known, and if he thought it would be known, perhaps he might not vote at all. In this view it would hardly be said to come within the meaning of the word 'intimidation.' Of course the principle laid down by the Minister of Justice is a good one, to use general words and not to specialize. To attempt to specialize and not specialize thoroughly, would result in more harm than good. But there is this to be said in favour of the standpoint of my hon. friend from Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) : He is speaking of something that has occurred in his own experience, he is speaking of a particular evil, and it would be possible to accomplish his amendment by providing that the special provision proposed as an amendment to the statute should not in any way restrict the effect of the general words which are used. I would like to understand from the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton), why it is that he repeals section 112, and I would like him to point out to me whether all the provisions of 112 are included in this Bill, or if not, why he thinks they are not necessary ?

Perhaps it would be better to dispose of this clause in the form in which we have it now, and when we reach that repealing clause, 112, it can be discussed. There are some verbal changes in this clause which I think are necessary.

In answer to the question asked by the leader of the opposition,
I may say that the transfer of the section 112 to this place was due to the fact that I considered the section specified an offence in the same line as the subsection from ' a ' to the one preceding this, and put it there for the purpose of having the provisions with regard to punishment on the next page, applicable to this as well as to the others. If this was condensed somewhat we might yet believe that it embodied all the provisions contained in section 112. But if that is not the case, section 112 as it stands upon the statute-book can be substituted for the language here. It was transferred here merely for the purpose of bringing it and the other offences under one general term.

In the last paragraph there is considerable change in the penalty. Two years is substituted for ' six months,' a penalty of $500 to $200, and there is disfranchisement for a period Mr. CLANCY.
of seven years under forfeiture of the charter. These provisions are entirely new. That clause will require careful consideration.

I want to point out that this section from the very beginning of subsection ' j ' would be much more effective if all the words after ' who ' in the lirst line of subsection ' j ' to the word ' impedes ' in the second line, were left out. I do not see why we sholuld limit the impeding, preventing, &c., to any particular sort of interference. It says:	' Every person
who by abduction, duress or any forcible or fraudulent device or contrivance, impedes.' Why should they impede at all ? Why should they impede, prevent or otherwise interfere with the free exercise of the elective franchise by any voter, in any way at all 1 One can see at once that a dozen cases might arise which a court would have to decide did not come within these words. I think the Minister of Justice will agree with me that if we would make the law effective, as we ought to try to do, we ought certainly to strike out these words so that if any one is impeded, prevented or otherwise interfered with in any way whatever there ought to be a penalty, instead of saying that the impeding must be done by ' abduction, duress or any forcible or fraudulent device or contrivance.' Any lawyer will see that you are hedging the prosecution around with many insuperable difficulties. I submit it would be much more effective, and better legislation, and would accomplish the object we have in view, if these words were struck out.

I think the House generally will agree that it is the desire of all parties to have an election law that is not only drastic, but one that will reach the various crimes that may be committed during, as well as prior to and subsequent to a political contest. There ought to be some provision that whenever a man, for any consideration, or under any promise, connives for an illegal purpose at getting information from another and in consideration of that information stifles the ends of justice, either in Canada or a foreign country, he ought to be punished. I find here that a case arose of that kind in the year 1899, and I propose to read to the House the evidence in order that the House may see the seriousness of the crime and the manner in which the information was procured.
Is it evidence ?

Mr. Watson next introduced the question of the Detroit affidavits, read by Mr. Whitney in the legislature. The first one was, the witness said, made by Judge Carpenter on December 29 last. It was prepared by Mr. Barker. It was prepared by Mr. Barker, a lawyer of Hamilton, a tall, thin man. The document was written in the hotel Cadillac. The parties met

by appointment, a note being left with Mr. Spence, with wholn witness was staying, fixing the place of mseting. Mr. Spence went with him; they met Mr. Barker and Mr. Fleming, of Windsor.
In reply to Barker, witness said he would make an affidavit under certain conditions.
Q. Under what conditions ?-A. That they would withdraw the warrant that was out against me ; they would protect me.
Q. How ?-A. By allowing me to go home ; have the warrant withdrawn and not prosecute me, or something to that effect.
Q. In consideration of what ?-A. That I would tell them what I knew about the West Elgin election.
Q. Have the warrants been withdrawn ?-A. So far as I know, I would not be here if they had not been.
Q. Have you seen the warrants since ?-A.
I saw them once in Windsor in Mr. Fleming's office.
That statement was made by me a few moments ago ; I made it upon the authority of the man who had made the sworn statement. The hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) has used rather strong language against me, even going so far, I think, as to call me a deliberate liar in stating what ITitchett swore to that he met the hon. member in Detroit, while if the bargain made at that meeting had been made in this country, would have rendered the member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) amenable to the criminal law.
I said a few moments ago distinctly that any man who makes the assertion which I understand the hon. member for South Sussex
Pritchett swore to it.

Any man, 1 do not care who or where he is, who makes the assertion that I ever promised to withdraw, or said one word to the effect that 1 would withdraw or procure the withdrawal of the warrant, or in any way interfere with the prosecution of Pritchett, or any other man, tells a deliberate falsehood. I saw the man Pritchett. He was about to make an affidavit and he did make the affidavit. He asked me in the presence of Mr. Fleming if, on behalf of the Conservative party, I would say that he should not be prosecuted. 1 told him distinctly half a dozen times that X would give him no such promise, that I could give him no such promise. I told him that the prosecution was in the hands of the Liberal party, that the county attorney of Elgin was a Liberal, and that if he wished to enforce the warrant he could do so.
How did you and Mr. Fleming get the warrant in your possession :
That statement that we got the warrant into our possession is an absolute falsehood. I never saw the warrant. I never heard of it- How would we get the warrant ?
From the constable ?
I did not know who the constable was.
The hon. member for East Elgin (Mr. Ingram) knows.
I said that the matter was in the hands of the county attorney of Elgin-a Liberal.
Not a Liberal.

I say this to the hon. member (Mr. Cowan) that I did not promise to withdraw that warrant or any other warrant. I repeat it in the strongest language- I do not care who says it or who repeats it It is an absolute untruth and there is not the slightest foundation for it.
What I stated was-
Give us Cap. Sullivan and his gang.
I do not know Cap. Sullivan, but apparently the hon. member for East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) does.
I have seen the blackguard with your ministers.

I have just had the first half of mine, Mr. Chairman. I want to be perfectly fair to the hon. member for Hamilton. All I can say is that Pritchett swore to it, that it was printed in every newspaper, that it was spoken of concerning the hon. member for Hamilton from many political platforms, and that it was brought up in this House. Yet, this is the first time that I have ever heard any contradiction of it. Pritchett swears that the hon. member for Hamilton prepared the affidavit and he swears that they had the warrant and had it at Windsor. However, I am prepared to accept the statement of the hon. member for Hamilton and to congratulate him that he is the first hon. gentleman on the other side of the House to join with us in saying that Pritchett was a liar, because, down to the present time, hon. gentlemen opposite have always declared that he was the most truthful gentleman that ever gave evidence.
Mr. Chairman-
