speechtext: I must urge hon. gentlemen
Oh, oh; fair play, fair play.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. My object is to bring the committee back to the work before it.
Go on ; go on.
The hon. member for South Essex says that I never denied it. I denied it- the first time the statement was ever made in my presence. He says further that the warrant was withdrawn in Windsor.

I made no such statement. I said that Pritchett said that he afterwards saw the warrant in Mr. Fleming's office, who was the gentleman who was with you when the affidavit was drawn and when you made the promise, if a promise was made.

I was never present in Mr. Fleming's office in Windsor and I cannot say whether that is true or not. I can only answer for what occurred when I was present. Pritchett was told positively that the warrant would not be withdrawn, that no effort would be made to withdraw it, and that if he returned to Canada he might be arrested so far as the Conservative party were concerned. I said : You will be arrested by the Liberals. He said :	Oh, I will
take the risk of being arrested by the Liberals. I dare them to arrest me.
They have not arrested him yet.

I would ask the mover of this Bill if section ' K ' applies to companies or corporations, such as railway companies. There is very grave doubt as to whether it really applies to corporations and if it docs not apply to them it is useless. It would appear that au employer may not do certain things but a foreman engaged by an employer might do all the things in this section and yet it would not apply.
Look at the fifth line on the second page, ' or in case the offense is committed by a corporation it shall forfeit its charter.'
That would not apply to the case I have mentioned.

A great deal of this kind of legislation in Ontario is a laughing stock, and whether our federal legislation on this matter is going to follow suit remains to be seen. While the hon. gentleman who introduced the Bill is not a lawyer, the Minister of Justice is, and the Minister of Justice must b 5 responsible to the people for such legislation as this. It would appear to me that the manager of a railway or even the foreman on a railway, being an employee, could not be got at under clause 'J.' I agree with the principle of the Bill because no one in this House suffers more from intimidation than the candidate in East Simcoe. There are two large public institutions in that riding and the grossest intimidation is practiced by the gentlemen who are in charge of these institutions under the local government. In addition, the lumbering concerns are as a rule adverse to the cause I represent. There should be a Mr. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
clause added to this Bill to meet such cases as that. I have known it to occur that on the day prior to ail election* the men were called before the mill at the dinner hour and were frankly told-this occurred in the local election-that owing to t'.ie numbers being on tlie ballots it would be known bow they voted, that there would be an officer of the compauy iu the poll to keep watch, and that in the interest of the company the men must support the Liberal candidate. That has also been done in the federal contest. The employer thinks that a more efficacious way than to issue a circular which might come up in evidence against him. If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Charlton) wants to meet such cases of intimidation as that he must amend his Bill. A deaf and dumb employer would be denied the privilege of suggesting to his men by letter or circular how ho wishes them to vote, but tlio employer who is fluent of speech can intimidate his men into voting as he wishes. But there is another view of this matter. Surely the lawT will not say that the owner of a manufacturing concern must not m conversation with his men express his opinion as to how-lie thinks the tariff for instance might affect his particular industry. That would be hampering the right of the individuals If this Bill really carries out the view the hon. gentleman (Mr. Charlton) seems to have, he would have to provide for the punishment of a manufacturer who at a public meeting expresses liis opinion as to what results a change of tariff would have on tlie particular industry with which he is concerned.
I submit that the Minister of Justice should have some opinion to give on this Bill.

I have been appealed to more than once but whenever I rose to reply some hon. gentleman had intervened to address the House. When this Bill was introduced I was under the Impression that it met with general acceptance and I was anxious to hear what should be said in favour of it. I was anxious that it should get into committee so that we might bear the details discussed. So far as my opinion is concerned of any value to this House I would say that the clauses of this Bill down to clause ' L ' provide for nothing that is not provided for by section 112, and that section 112 provides for many things that are not provided for by this Bill. The difficulty suggested about the employer, or the employee or the foremen would be met by section 112, and it is not met by this Bill.
That is a very good reason why in the case of Bills of this character the clauses which it is proposed to amend should be printed so that we know what we are doing.

I did not intend this Bill to get out ot committee with-

out saying what I had to say about it. Some people pretended to be very virtuous when this Bill was introduced, and anxious that it should become law, and I was waiting until my time came to express an opinion about it.

It occurred to me that the Bill -was in the right direction but whether it -was not already provided for by law I was unable to say. I have had occasion to study tile Election Act pretty frequently but I confess that I cannot carry out all its clauses in my head. If the clauses which it is sought to amend were printed we would know what we are doing.

Some thing may be said in favour of subsections ' L ' and ' N ' of subsection 1, but that is all I think that would be useful In the Bill. The provision in subsection 2 is better met under the Canada Evidence Act. Section 4 goes too far and will fail entirely of the purpose my hon. friend (Mr. Charlton) has in view I expected to hear the Bill fully discussed in committee, and then to ask that the committee should rise and at a future date I might have some statement to make in connection with the Bill.
To whom did the Minister of Justice refer to as being very virtuous and wishing the Bill to pass ?
I would rather not pursue that matter any further.

Our object on this side of the House is to make the Bill as efficient as possible. Some time ago I myself made the suggestion which the Minister of Justice has now made that subsections ' J ' and ' K ' do not embody all the provisions of section 112, I think that the Minister of Justice should be able to tell us now what is the policy of the government in regard to this. A public Bill of this kind is under the control of the government and should be dealt with by the government, and I expected that the Minister of Justice would place before us for consideration the amendments which he thought ought to be made. My hon. friend the Minister of Justice has not done that. I think he ought to do it as being responsible for legislation of this character. That is to say, he should come here witli a suggestion of amendments which the government think ought to be made in this Bill and let the Committee have a chance of considering them. I fully agree that we cannot pass the Bill in just its present form, though I am not clear as to my concurrence in some of the suggestions which the hon. Minister of Justice has made. The Bill will require considerable amendment before it is passed. In saying that I am sincerely desirous of assisting the hon. gentleman who has introduced it in his very good intention of making the election law more effective. But I would like to know whether the government have had under consideration the two possible amendments which I suggested on the motion for the second reading of the Bill. One is the appointment of an officer to fill the position of public prosecutor under the election law, who should be placed in the same independent position as the Auditor General now ocupies. The other, which would be more pertinent as an amendment to the Franchise Act, is to provide that any man who does not see fit to exercise his franchise shall not have the opportunity of exercising it for some time thereafter. I think the two sides of the House might meet on common ground with regard to some of these matters, and do much to remedy a condition of affairs that is not creditable to either political party in Canada.

I would like, before the Committee rises, to have this added to the Bill :
That any person known to subscribe to an election fund shall be liable to a fine of not less than $500 and to be imprisoned for not less than six months, with or without hard labour.

With reference to the remarks of my hon. friend the leader of the opposition, I always carefully consider to the best of my ability legislation of this sort before it is brought before the House. At the same time, I do not think it would be right or proper for me to express a final or settled opinion until I hear all that is to be said on the measure. I come here for the purpose of listening to the discussion. I have my opinions, but they are not, like the laws of the Medes and Persians, unalterable. I come here for light, and perhaps, after I hear further discussion, I may change some of my opinions. I wish to have the measure discussed by men who, from their _ experience in election courts, can give light on many of these matters; and when it is fully discussed, my intention is to ask the Committee to rise and report progress, so that I may have an opportunity of considering nil that has been said, and. when the Committee meets again. I may have some statement to make to the House.

My hon. friend's remarks have reference, and very properly, to this particular Bill. My own view, speaking for myself-and I do not think my colleague will dissent from it-is that the representatives of the people on both sides, by a special committee, ought to take into consideration the question how we might amend the electoral law so as to avoid those evils which have received so much prominence in the past. I am glad to hear the hon. leader of the opposition speak in the same sense to-day. It is not worth while for ns to make recriminations across the House in regard to the conduct of elections. We must recognize, from the revelations of the election courts, that there

have been manifestations in connection with elections which must be a cause of regret to men on both sides; and if we approach the subject dispassionately, with a desire to bring about some improvement, I think something might be done. One view I have held so strongly that it has been called a fad, is that the courts should themselves take cognizance of an election without waiting for a petition. The judges might investigate an election, say within one month or two months after it took place, while it is fresh in the public mind, and while men are ready to bring forward evidence if they have it. The present method of requiring a petition to be filed is open to objection. For instance, it is wrong to fine a man a thousand dollars before allowing him to file a petition. If there has been corruption in an election, we ought not to put difficulties in the way of an investigation, which is done as the law now stands. It might lie difficult to get the judges to perform the duty I suggest; but after all, while some of the judges are overworked, a considerable number of them have ample time to undertake it. They would not wait for a petition, but the investigation would be compulsory. Then, when I went into an election campaign, I would go into it with the fact before my eyes that shortly afterwards my conduct would be investigated.
What does the hon. gentleman think of compulsory voting ?

Compulsory voting in the ordinary sense of the word we should hesitate to enforce; but such compulsory voting as has been referred to this afternoon is, I think, well worthy of consideration; that is, that if an elector does not think enough of the franchise to cast his vote, his name should be left off the list for some time afterwards. To that extent I would favour compulsory voting. Many of these questions present difficulties, but we are here to try to solve these difficulties, and I am persuaded that if hon. gentlemen on both sides, instead of fighting each other, united to devise the best remedy for the evils referred to, we could accomplish much good. With regard to the trading off of election petitions, it does seem a public scandal; but on the other hand one-half of the petitions are filed without any knowledge or information, and there is no great harm in withdrawing them. But with a proper administration of our election laws, we might save a great deal of scandal and trouble that now exists. We should make an attempt in a non-partisan spirit, and if our hon. friends opposite will receive the suggestion in that spirit, we would be glad to meet them in a committee and endeavour to bring about a reform in the law, not simply to the extent to which the hon. member for North Norfolk desires, but beyond that in other directions that may make for purity in elections.

MONK (Jacques Cartier) moved the second reading of Bill (No. 18) to amend the Interpretation Act. He said :	Mr. Speaker, the Bill the second reading of which I have the honour to move was suggested to me by the sensation, if I may use such an expression, which was created in the province of Quebec at the time of the rendering of the judgment of the Privy Council in the case of Roy vs. the Canadian

Pacific Railway Company. When I have stated the facts in that case as briefly as possible, the House will at once understand the object of the Bill under consideration. Roy was a farmer in the province of Quebec. His barn was in the neighbourhood of the Canadian Pacific Railway. The barn was consumed by fire, and Roy sought to recover damages from the Canadian Pacific Railway Company on the ground that his barn had been ignited by a spark from one of the locomotives of the company. He brought his action in the Supreme Court of the province of Quebec. The court of original jurisdiction rendered judgment in favour of Roy for the sum of $300. Mr. Justice Langelier, of the Superior Court, who heard the case in the first instance, and whosei judgment, as well as the judgment of the Court of Appeals, which was rendered subsequently, can be found in the Law reports, appeals cases, 1902, at page 220, held that the fire) had been caused by a spark from a locomotive of the Canadian Pacific Railway and one of his considera-ants or motives, reads as follows :
Considering that the circumstances unfolded in the case leave no doubt that the fire was kindled either by sparks escaping from the locomotive or by fire thrown in some other way from the train;
Considering that there thence results a presumption of negligence or carelessness on the parts of the defendant's employees in charge of the train, and that it was the defendants' duty to negative this presumption, which they have npt done ;
Considering that the defendants were responsible for damages caused to the plaintiff by the fire ;
-and the judge gave Roy a decree as I have said, for the sum of $300. An appeal to the Court of Queen's Bench in the province of Quebec was taken on the ground that, in fact and on the finding of the court below, it was not shown that the fire was caused by any act on the part of the appellant or their employees and also that the complainant had not proved negligence and that they were not liable by law. The Court of Appeals of the province of Quebec held that the Canadian Pacific Railway was responsible in spite of its proof, which the Court of Appeals considered satisfactory, that, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company had adopted all the modern appliances necessary to prevent accidents by fire arising from sparks issuing from the smokestacks of their locomotives. In spite of this fact and of the argument, very strongly urged on the part of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company that, having proved that they had taken every precaution and having been authorized by parliament to run their trains, they were not responsible for damages caused by the running of their trains, the Court of Appeals of the province of Quebec, considering that the defendants while authorized to operate their trains,! are, nevertheless, liable to damages which the exercise of this right may cause,
and, that, in this regard they are subject to the rules of liability fixed in this province, by the civil law of this province, affirm the judgment of the Superior Court. I may say here, for the information of the House, that the Court of Appeals based its judgment on the following articles of our civil code for lower Canada :
Article 356: civil corporations constituting, by the fact of their incorporation, ideal or artificial persons, are as such governed by the laws affecting individuals; saving the privileges they enjoy and the disabilities they are subject to.
Article 1053. Every person capable of discerning right from wrong is responsible for the damage caused by his fault to another, whether by positive act, imprudence, neglect or want of skill.
Article 1054. He is responsible not only for the damage caused by his own fault, but also for that caused by the fault of persons under his control .	.	. Masters and employers are responsible for the damage caused by their servants and workmen in the performance of the work for which they are employed.
Now, let me quote the remarks of Mr. Justice Hall in rendering the judgment of the Court of Appeals in the province of Quebec, as reported in the law reports- of appeal cases :
The appellants' argument is that as parliament has given to them the statutory power to use locomotives for hauling their trains, the necessary use of fire in them, and the occasional escape of sparks from them, must have been anticipated, and therefore, if every reasonable precaution is taken against such escapes the railway companies are relieved, in advance, of the consequence of any fire resulting from sparks accidentally escaping.
The appellants admit that at common law they would be responsible for damage to others caused by fires from their locomotives, irrespective of the question of negligence on their part, but contend that the statute, by authorizing the use of locomotives, has taken away the common law liability, and left them responsible only for the effect of negligence. The English authorities support this position, commencing with the case of Rex v. Pease (1), followed by Vaughan v. Taff Vale Railway Company (3), Fletcher v. Rylands (3), Smith v. London and Southwestern Railway Company (4), and lastly, the important case of Port Glasgow and Newark Sailcloth Company v. Caledonian Railway (5), with the report of which we have been favoured by Appellants' counsel, as found in 30 S.L.R. 587 (6), in which it was held : that the legislature by authorizing the use of steam engines on railways, has impliedly indemnified railway companies against the consequence of the use of such engines, provided they are of the best construction and that the proper safeguards are used for minimizing the risk of fire damage.
The same principle has evidently been fol-lowered in those provinces of the Dominion in which the English law has been adopted, and by our Supreme Court in cases which originated in such provinces.
Mr. Justice Hall proceeds as follows
The appellants have conclusively established, we think that the principle for which they contend is supported by English jurisprudence

wherever that jurisprudence is in force, but in a matter pertaining to civil rights end liabilities in this province we are controlled by a different authority, which is binding upon us whenever it conflicts with the law of England, as it does upon this question, and under that authority we are of opinion that a different rule prevails. As Mr. Holt clearly puts the matter in his Canadian Railway Law, page 18:
' The French law, and consequently the law in the province of Quebec, is that the (railway) company is always responsible, notwithstanding the adoption by them of every means of precaution known to science. Upon such question it is our duty to refer to the French jurisprudence and text writers, not that that country dictates or enforces our laws, but because our civil laws were derived from France, and find therefore, its best exponents. Their jurisprudence is uniform and conclusive, and proceeds upon a principle derived from the Roman law which must commend itself to all as both equitable and just, namely, that no one may use his property in such a way as to injure that of his neighbour, ' Sic utere tuo ut alieo ne lmdas' and the French authors carry this principle so far as to contend that even the legislature has not power to violate it, and that whenever it confers special privileges upon an individual or a company, the reserve in favour of the neighbours rights must be understood to have been intended.
Mr. Justice Boss6 spoke very much in the same terms. I may say that the judges of the Court of Appeal in the province of Quebec, in delivering this judgment, referred at great length to our constant jurisprudence in the province of Quebec upon that very subject. The cases which they quoted are reported at length in our own report, but they are summarized in this very full report, the Law Reports of Appeal Cases, 1902, page 220, the case of Roy. I will endeavour to be as short as possible and not go more fully into what was held by the Court of Appeal, as I think the House sufficiently understands that point. The case was taken to the Privy Council on the ground, X suppose, that rights in future might be affected, because the amount of the judgment was only $300. The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council unanimously recommended that the judgment be set aside and the appeal maintained, and Roy's action was dismissed. It was dismissed without costs, because costs had not been asked for. The Lord Chancellor spoke as follows :-
The serious and important question sought to be raised in this appeal is whether the railway company, authorized by statute to carry on their railway undertaking in the place and by means that they do carry it on, are responsible in damage for injuries not caused by negligence but by the ordinary and normal use of their railway.
Both courts below have held that in the province of Quebec the railway company is so responsible and the question is whether that is the law.
The argument appears to be founded on the suggestion that Quebec has a civil law of its own, and that in that province all corporations like all other persons are responsible for causing damage to their neighbours by a fault- Mr. MONK.
that is to say, any actionable wrong, whether imprudence or want of skill ; and another article of the Code provides that civil corporations constituting by the fact of their incorporation ideal or artificial persons are as such governed by the laws affecting individuals, having the privileges they enjoy and the disabilities they are subjected to.
If the immunity claimed for the appellant were simply claimed upon the ground that they were a corporation without reference to what they are authorized to do in that capacity, the argument would be well founded; but the fallacy of the suggestion lies in supposing that immunity is claimed because they are a corporation. If it were so, there would be no difference between the law of England and 1he law as so expounded in the province of Quebec ; but the ground upon which the immunity of a railway company for injury caused by the normal use of their line is based is that the legislature, which is supreme, has authorized the particular thing so done in the place and by the means contemplated by the legislature, and that cannot constitute an actionable wrong in England any more than it can constitute a fault by the Quebec Code.
Further on the Lord Chancellor says
This permission

That is to say, the authorization of parliament to run a railroad.
This permission, of course, does not authorize the thing to be done negligently or even unnecessarily to cause damage to others. Much was argued by the learned counsel for the respondent as to the peculiar jurisprudence of Quebec, but in truth there is no such difference between the law of England and the law of Quebec in this respect as he seemed to suppose. The law of England, equally with the law of the province in question, affirms the maxim * Sic utere tuo ut alieo ne laedas.' But the previous state of the law, whether in Quebec, or France, or England, cannot render inoperative the positive enactment of a statute, and the whole case turns, not upon what was a common law of either country, but what is the true construction of plain words authorizing the doing of the very thing complained of.
The legislature is supreme and if it has enacted that a thing is lawful, such a thing cannot be a fault or an actionable wrong. The thing to be done is a privilege as well as a right and duty, and it seems to the Lordships it comes within the expressed language of the code (article 35G).
Now, Mr. Speaker, what I desire to call attention to is the fact that, as indicated by the remarks of the judges who delivered judgment in the Superior Court as well as in the Court of Appeal in our own province, there has never been any variance in our own province as to the principle hitherto prevailing there, namely, that persons or corporations, as in the present case, even when exercising a right, or doing something which has been expressly authorized by statute, if in the exercise of that right those persons or companies commit a wrong or cause damage, they are responsible for those damages. The jurisprudence in our own province has been uniform upon that point, and it sems to me, with all due re-

spect to the judgment rendered by their Lordships in the Privy Council, and it has seemed to a great many lawyers and judges in our own province, that this is the correct interpretation of our own law. The judgments in our own province have been uniform, and they are based upon holdings of the French courts, the highest courts in France, which, as Mr. Justice Hall said, in delivering the judgment of the Court of Appeals, are not binding upon us excepting in so far as they serve to interpret the principles of a system of law which is the same as that which prevails in our own province.
Therefore, I say that the jurisprudence in France as well as in the province of Quebec is uniform upon this subject. The bon. Minister of Justice, in a very exhaustive and able article which was published in one of our legal monthly publications, ' La Revue Legale,' goes very fully into the study of the case of Roy vs. the Canadian Pacific Railway Company which, as I stated in the beginning, has created a very widespread interest among the legal fraternity and I might almost say among the general public in the province of Quebec. The lion. Minister of Justice in that article quotes the two judgments rendered in France which, to a very large extent, insofar as they are to be considered as precedents, or expositions of the system of law, which is our own to a very large extent, held precisely as our courts have held. The case which has frequently been quoted before our own tribunals is the case of the First Chamber of the Imperial Court of Bordeaux which reversed the judgments of the imperial courts in France and held, as it has been held in our own courts unanimously in the province of Quebec, that, even where a railway company in France is authorized to carry on the operations of a railway company, to run trains with all the danger that it entails, even when duly authorized in every respect and observing all the precautions possible to avoid accidents, if a railway locomotive sets fire to a building in the( course of its operations the railway company is responsible. That is the decision of the Imperial Court of Bordeaux rendered in 1859. The second decision is the decision of the Tribunal of the Seine, also in 1859. I will not quote fully either of these judgments, though I intended to do so, but they hold absolutely the contrary of what was held by the Privy Council i'n this case of Roy. It is evident that in these cases the companies pleaded that they -were exercising the right authorized by the supreme authority of the land and that they exercised that right with all due precaution; nevertheless, under the articles of the French code, very similar, if not absolutely identical to our own in reference to torts, they were held responsible. I will also quote from an author who is a very high authority: indeed, he is the highest on questions of damages-Laurent.	Laurent,
one of our best commentators, referring to
the case of locomotives setting fire to buildings, exactly as in the case of Roy, says :
Fire, or sparks which escape trom locomotives often produce fires. Are companies in such case responsible ? There can be no doubt as to the affirmative answer to this question when the accident is produced by faulty construction of the locomotive. When the locomotive is provided with proper appliances to prevent the issuing of sparks out of the smokestack the question is more doubtful.
And he proceeds to quote the decision of the Bordeaux Court, adding :
One applies, in a case of this kind, the principles which regulate dangerous establishments. It would he useless for the company to invoke as an excuse the authorization which it has received to execute its works. The court will answer that the state has not conceded the right to cause damages.
My hon. friend the Minister of Justice, in this paper, seems to arrive at the conclusion, nevertheless, that there is no such authority in France as corresponds with our own parliament, particularly with the limitless authority which our parliaments have exercised, certainly, for a hundred years and as there is, according to the argument of the lion. Minister of Justice, no authority In France having the paramount strength which our parliament has, we cannot compare the jurisprudence of France with our own on a question of this kind. Well, the answer to that seems to me that although, as a matter of public law, if I say use that expression, the law making authority in France is not, in many respects, similar to the law making authority which we have here under British institutions, nevertheless, there is no doubt that in France railway companies, to exercise their rights, require the sanction of some supreme authority without which they cannot exercise those rights any more than railway companies can exercise them in our own country, and that, therefore, there is more analogy than this article of the hon. Minister of Justice would lead one to believe, there is more reason to give strength and value to the jurisprudence of France than at first sight one would think from the consideration invoked by the hon. Minister of Justice. But, at any rate, there can be no question as to what has obtained hitherto in our own country. The jurisprudence is all in the direction which I indicated as being the direction adopted by the Court of Appeals, when it decided the case of Roy. I do not say, for my own part, that, even admitting that there is a difference between the absolute and paramount authority of our parliament, and the authority which the administration possesses in France, it makes any difference in regard to the responsibility in a case such as the case of Roy. because, the principle which the Court of Appeal of the province of Quebec adopted in the case of Roy, was : that under our civil law the relation between a private individual such as Roy and a company such

as the Canadian Pacific Railway authorized to carry on its operations, is a relation which springs absolutely from our civil law-it is not governed by any principle of public law, but it is a relation which is governed absolutely by the principles of our civil code. And if we adopt these principles and adhere strictly to the doctrine of all our authors as to that relation ; even if the parliament of Canada has power to grant the most extensive privileges to a railway company or a telegraph company, or a company of any kind, nothing can disturb that relation as established by our Civil Code. Otherwise one would have to arrive at the conclusion that the civil relations which are entirely under the control of our provincial legislature, would be disturbed in every instance where the parliament of Canada has authorized the doing of certain things, and persons or companies enjoying the authorization of the parliament of Canada or of the Quebec legislature under this idea of a paramount authority, would be in a more advantageous position in regard to their civil relations with individuals than would ordinary persons who would not enjoy that special statutory advantage. That I think is contrary to justice and contrary to law. I am not going to attempt to discuss at length the question raised by the Minister of Justice in this interesting paper published by him; I shall not endeavour to establish before this House the principle, that under our law there was a civil responsibility in such a case as the Roy case. I proceed upon the principle that the interpretation given by our own courts to our own law is a proper interpretation, and that the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council if it held that it was not the law of our province, was mistaken ; which is a possibility which has happened already, because we know that in certain cases-rare cases it is true-the Privy Council has reversed its own decisions. Taking as the point of departure, that that is our law, this Bill is the solution which I have endeavoured to apply to this question. It is impossible, of course, and it would be improper, to seek to change the judgment rendered by the Lords of the Privy Council, but after consultation with many lawyers in my province and some judges, we have come to the conclusion that to avoid the happening of such things in the future as happened in the Roy case, it would be a proper thing to amend section 7 of the Interpretation Act, in order to emphasize the fact that in Canada property and civil rights are subject entirely to the jurisdiction of the province. I will quote the article of the Interpretation Act which this Bill is intended to amend, and I may say that in any event it seems to me that the amendment of the Interpretation Act can do nothing but good in the future. Article 7 says :
In every Act of the parliament of Canada, unless the context otherwise requires :-

(1.) The enactments apply to the whole of Canada.
(2.) No Act amending a previous Act which does not apply to all the provinces of Canada, and no enactments in any such amending Act, although of a substantive nature or form, shall apply to any province to which the amended Act does not apply, unless it is expressly provided that such amending Act or enactment shall apply to such province or to all the provinces of Canada.
The Bill which I propose amends paragraph 1 of section 7, and the section as amended would read as follows :
In every Act of the parliament of Canada unless the context otherwise provides : The enactments apply to the whole of Canada : Provided always, that no right, power or privilege conferred by an Act of the parliament of Canada, or by a charter granted under an Act of that parliament, shall exempt any person exercising that right, power or privilege, from any liability incurred by him under any Act of a legislature or under the common law.
This means that under section 7 as amended, there would be an affirmation In express terms, that no power granted by an Act of the parliament of Canada or by a charter, shall exempt any person exercising that right, power or privilege from any liability incurred under the law of the province relating to property and civil rights. That disposition of the Interpretation Act shall apply generally not only to railway companies, but to telegraph companies, electric companies and all industrial companies as to which there may be legislation in the future, and courts called upon to decide questions of tort or damage must take into consideration that clear indication in the law as amended, that whatever power the parliament of Canada can confer, it in no way interferes with the disposition of the law of one of the provinces under section 92 of the British North America Act, which reserves exclusively to the province the control as to property and civil rights. I do not know that it is possible for us here to go further than this. My hon. friend from St. John and Iberville (Mr. Demers) has an Act before the House which I suppose I may say has been suggested by this same case of Roy.
My hon. friend in that Bill proposes a different remedy which at first sight seems very acceptable to those who believe, as we in the province of Quebec, that railway companies, even when exercising a statutory right, are nevertheless liable for the damages which they cause. The enactment proposed by my hon. friend from St. John and Iberville is that the railway companies shall be absolutely responsible for fires caused by their locomotives. But what I submit to this House is that by an enactment of that kind we are invading the legislative domain which by our constitution is reserved absolutely to the provinces. We are enacting a law having reference to property and civil rights, and I question very much

if that enactment would not be considered ultra vires of this legislature; and it presents this other feature, in that it imposes upon the other provinces a system of law as to tort and damages which has never prevailed there; because, I take it, although I am not familiar with their systems of law, that in the other provinces of this Dominion the rule of law laid down by the Privy Council in the case of Roy is the rule which prevails everywhere. It is only in the province of Quebec, under the system of the old Roman law and the French civil law, that we are in a certain sense exceptionally and advantageously situated in regard to fires such as happen in the case of Roy; and it is deemed important in our province that we should preserve that disposition of the law which requires railway companies to indemnify farmers and others whose barns are set fire to by the operation of the railways, whether they are exercising a statutory right or not. In other words, I have been induced to bring in this Bill in order to emphasize, if possible, the guarantee which our civil law gives in cases such as the one now under consideration. How far this Bill may succeed in preserving that privilege I do not know. I would be quite prepared to adopt any other remedy of a practical nature that might be suggested. But after careful consideration of the question, and after submitting that question to the consideration of a great number of persons in my province who are more conversant than I am with the intricacies of our law, they have come to the conclusion that the Bill now submitted to the House is the most effectual remedy that can be provided under the circumstances. At any rate, that Bill, by extending the provisions of the Interpretation Act, and by emphasizing the principle that any enactment of this legislature should not interfere with the enactments properly made of our own legislature, can do no harm. Therefore, I think the Bill ought to commend itself to the consideration of this House.

speakername: The SOLICITOR GENERAL (Hon. H. G. Carroll).

speechtext: I do not dispute that.

I understood that the hon. gentleman did dispute it. At all events, the whole trend of his argument was that we should not interfere with matters of property and civil rights, which should be left to the province. That im.pression has been created by the discussion which took place here last session, so much so that the Minister of Justice has been accused in the press of being an enemy of the French civil law of the province of Quebec.
I thought that what the hon. gentleman has been stating is an elementary principle which has been well recognized for many years.
It settles this argument if it is.
It does not settle this matter of legislation, because this parliament can refrain from doing what it has the power to do.

The hon. gentleman has admitted that his Bill is the result of the judgment of the Privy Council in the case of Roy vs. the Canadian Pacific Railway. The Privy Council decided that when a railway company had taken all possible means to prevent fire, and when it was shown that there was no negligence on its part, the company was not responsible. This is not the first case in which this principle has been affirmed. It was affirmed in the case of Vaughan vs. Taff Vale Railway Company, the same principle was affirmed. The court held :
Although it may be true that if a person keep an animal of known dangerous propensities. or a dangerous instrument, he will be responsible to those who are thereby injured, independently of any negligence in the mode of dealing with the animal or using the instrument; yet when the legislature has sanctioned or authorized the use of a particular thing, and it is used for the purpose for which it was authorized and every precaution has been observed to prevent injury, the sanction of the legislature carries with it this consequence : that if the damage results from the use of any such thing, independently of negligence, the party using it is not responsible.
This is the same doctrine as that which lms been laid down in the case of Roy vs. the Canadian Pacific Railway. The courts of the province of Quebec, however, have hitherto leaned towards the doctrine that railway companies are responsible irrespective of negligence, but my hon. friend must not forget that in France a law was passed in 1845 which, while of course maintaining the liability of railway companies, limits that liability. Article 7 of the Law of the 12th July, 1845, forbids the placing of less than sixty feet from a railway of thatched roofs or other deposits of an inflammable nature :
Section 7 of the Law of July 15, 1865, prohibits the placing, within a distance of twenty metres from the track of a railway, of thatched roofs, hay.-stacks or any other materials of an inflammable nature.
Does that law affect us ?
It affects the interpretation of our Quebec civil law.
It has been argued by the hon. gentleman and others that when a building is destroyed by a fire caused by sparks from a locomotive, it is

just as much expropriated as it could be under the ordinary process of law, and it was only equitable that the proprietor should be given compensation, but is this contingency affected by the Bill now before the House ? The Privy Council has declared that when they give a charter to a railway company, that carries with it a privilege. Should the hon. gentleman's Bill pass, the right which the company enjoy under this privilege would remain absolutely the same.

Supposing we incorporate an electric company and in carrying out the powers granted to it by our parliament, observing all due precautions, that electric company causes damage, does my hon. friend not think that in an action to recover our courts would to a certain extent, be guided by the affirmation of a principle contained id this enactment.

I am arguing the effect of the Bill of the hon. gentleman in the light of the judgment of the Privy Council. The Privy Council has decided that when we grant a charter we grant a privilege and the hon. gentleman's Bill provides :
(1.) The enactments apply to the whole of Canada : Provided always, that no right, power or privilege conferred by an Act of the parliament of Canada, or by a charter granted under an Act of that parliament, shall exempt any person exercising that right, power or privilege, from any liability incurred by him under any Act of a legislature or under the common law.
Supposing this law should pass, it will not affect the interpretation given those laws by the Privy Council. Our Quebec courts have decided that railway companies are responsible under our civil law, but the Privy Council has decided that they are not. It Is wholly a question of interpretation, and even should this Bill pass the) Privy Council will still decide that when we grant a charter to a railway company, we grant a privilege, and that privilege relieves the company of responsibility according to our civil law as it now stands. Of course if the legislatures change the law as to liability, then their legislation may clash with our legislation, and this may have serious consequences. I am in sympathy with the object of the hon. gentleman but I do not think that this Bill will accomplish it. I am rather disposed to think that the Bill of my hon. friend from St. John and Iberville (Mr. Demers) will be more effective. I am therefore of the opinion that the Bill of the hon. gentleman should not pass, but that the House should rather consider the Bill of my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Demers).

speakeroldname: Mr. L. P. DEMERS (St. John and Iberville).
speechtext:
(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, I have placed upon the Order Paper a Bill, the object of which is similar to that aimed at by the Bill introduced by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk), which is

under discussion. I may perhaps be allowed briefly to explain the reasons why I have introduced this Bill, notwithstanding the tact that the hon. gentleman's Bill was already on the Order Paper. As just remarked by the hon. Solicitor General (Mr. Carroll), the object aimed at by the hon. gentleman from Jacques Cartier is not likely to be readied by the measure which he has introduced. Indeed, this Bill enacts, that, notwithstanding any provision to the contrary, any Act of the parliament of Canada must be so interpreted that it shall not exempt any person from any liability incurred by him under any Act of a provincial legislature.
The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council has dealt with the matter. Had their Lordships declared that the laws of the province of Quebec did not apply, I grant that the amendment to the Interpretation Act, embodied in the hon. gentleman's Bill would attaiu the object sought. But the Privy Council have based their judgment on the Civil Code of the province of Quebec and they have said : ' The Dominion parliament grants a certain privilege to railway companies, and under section 356 of the Civil Code civil corporations, constituting by the fact of their incorporation real or artificial persons, are as such governed by 'Vue'laws	icCrriig * rifdivfanils, saving 'tut
privileges they enjoy under their charter. Hence it follows that, under the Civil Code, the privilege granted railway companies to carry on their business and operate their railways by means of locomotives is recognized beyond a doubt, and I believe the Bill introduced by my hon, friend does not provide a remedy. The Bill which I have brought down does not apply solely to the province of Quebec, but its object is to provide a common law as to the liability of railway companies, which shall apply to all the provinces of the Dominion.
The common law says that if I set fire to my property I am responsible for damage to a neighbour's property. That is the common law in Great Britain, in the United States and in all the provinces of the Dominion as well. The judgment rendered by the Privy Council does not say anything to the contrary, and the reason why the decision of our courts was set aside, not that our common law conflicts with the English common law, but because the power of our parliament is paramount. A railway company which is empowered by its charter to operate its line and to use locomotives for hauling its trains, is responsible, in common law, for damages to others from sparks emitted from locomotive engines. Therefore, it is in virtue of its charter that the company may claim a privilege conflicting with the common law.
Now, the object of my Bill is to say which is the common law that shall apply to all the provinces. So. I submit that the Bill introduced by my hon. friend does not 30
meet the case we are now dealing with.
I may perhaps be told that this has nothing to do with civil rights in the provinces. The answer to that objection is that the Railway Act embodies many provisions relating to property. For instance, you will find in the Railway Act provisions concerning land expropriations, which is beyond doubt a matter pertaining to civil rights. I may add that, during this session, we have had a Bill before this House, to the effect of providing compensation for owners of cattle, when there are no proper cattle-guards.
From session to session, within the last few years, we had this Bill before us, and I am not aware that any question as to whether it was intra vires of this parliament has ever been raised. From what I have said it follows that the only remedy is the one proposed in my Bill, namely, that recourse should be had to this parliament, within whose jurisdiction it is to remove all doubts as to privileges granted under charters obtained from parliament.

It is, of course, clearly laid down and has been plainly announced not only by the Privy Council, but in parliament that, in those matters over which this parliament has control, as in bankruptcy or insolvency or similar matters, it has the right to make all necessary provisions for the purposes of carrying out



Its legislation. For instance, it provides the procedure in respect of bankruptcy, and makes other necessary provisions which will occur to every lawyer who has considered the matter at all. Then, it necessarily follows that, in dealing with matters of this kind you must Interfere with civil rights and the jurisdiction of parliament to interfere with civil rights to that extent is undoubted, and has been so for a long time. It is quite competent for parliament to limit its legislation in that regard, as I suggested to my hon. friend the Solicitor General (Hon. Mr. Carroll), and, in doing so, to provide that the making of that enactment shall not extend beyond a certain limit so far as concerns its interference with civil rights. I do not think any person would doubt that. It would be competent for the parliament of Canada in making an enactment in regard to a railway or anything else to provide that the Act should not extend beyond a certain limit in its interference with civjl rights. That is all I meant by an interruption to which the lion. Minister of Justice (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick) made some allusion. Now, the common law of England as announced in the recent decisions-that is, decisions within the last fifty years-is that the right to construct and operate a railway in a certain place is a bar against civil liability to any person injured by it, in the absence of negligence. And as the Solicitor General says, it must be shown to the court that the railway company has not employed the most improved appliances to prevent damage. That is not a principle applicable to railways alone, but to other similar works. A great many decisions during the last twenty five or thirty years have been given with regard to the erection of gas works. Very often the application of the principle depends upon the particular language of the statute. To every one who has had occasion to examine very closely the decisions with regard to this matter it will be plain on what very slight foundation the jurisprudence with regard to railways rested in the first instance. It depends very often upon the question whether the particular manufactory or railway is authorized in a particular place. A general power, for example, to erect a gas works does not necessarily give power to erect a gas works in a residential part of the city. But if you have power under the statute to erect a gas works or any other manufactory creating nuisance in a particular place, another result might follow^. The criticism that might fairly be offered to the language of the Bill is not exactly, it seems to me, on the lines suggested by the Solicitor General ? He does not seem to think that it is language that could amount to anything. On the contrary, it seem to me too comprehensive. It might have the effect of nullifying many Acts passed by this legislature.
Absolutely.
If it means anything it means that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It might be open to that argument, as I was suggesting privately to my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk). The hon. gentleman tells me that the Bill was drafted by other gentlemen and placed in his hands and his attention had not been directed to that. I think it is perfectly easy to deal with this matter from the standpoint of my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier, but I would be inclined to think, as I have suggested, that this may carry it too far.
All I said was, that so far as the Quebec law is concerned, the language of the amendment would make no difference-the law would be the same.

I would not make any suggestion as to the Quebec law. I do not pretend to understand that. I do not know whether it would make a difference in the law of Quebec or not. But It seems to me it would have the effect of very materially altering the law not only for other provinces, but for Quebec also. A right or privilege may be given by statute but you come to the Interpretation Act and find it is taken away by this particular provision. For example, you find that an officer of the customs has a right to enter a house under certain circumstances and make a search. But you might find under this provision that he is not saved from the action for damages taken by the party whose house he has entered.
And that which is declared by us to be a privilege might be an actionable wrong under the local legislature.
Or under the common law.
That wmuld be an anomaly for which we ought not to be responsible.

In dealing with the question whether this Bill ought to be passed or not, it is a question whether, assuming that it would be right to restore the law of Quebec to what it was supposed to be, this Bill -would not require considerable amendment before it should pass the House.

I should be a little reluctant
to express any opinion on this subject as raised by the hon. member's Bill, having had only a little while-since the discussion commenced-to turn it over in my mind. But I have been very much puzzled to find what limitations would be placed on the

Bill of the hon. gentleman. So far as 1 have been able to get at the meaning and effect of the language, particularly in the concluding portion of the clause, it would seem that parliament would be recognizing that what it granted with one hand it was, in an indirect manner through its Interpretation Act, taking away with the other. It would seem that while parliament was endeavouring to regulate the liabilities which attached necessarily to the exercise of the privilege Which it was conferring, it was at the same time, in explicit terms, recognizing that other liabilities which it had no hand at all in regulating, and which were necessary to the proper exercise of the privilege conferred, could be created by another legislative body or bodies, either to cut into or to supplement the liabilities which parliament itself, and the courts Interpreting the Act of parliament, considered would only attach to it. I do not know whether I make myself clear, but it is very much in the line of the trouble which suggests itself to the mind of the hon. the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Borden). They say here that no authority or privilege conferred by parliament shall exempt any person exercising that law from any liability which the legislature may attach to its exercise, 'or which the common law would attach to its exercise. The legislature might make an enactment which would be in its operation and effect distinctly contrary to the intention of parliament. Parliament might say that under the railway charter a company might go on and expropriate lands under certain conditions; the legislature might say that if lands are expropriated by any railway company, and civil rights are interfered with, and property taken, such and such responsibilities must attach. I do not wish to speak too decidedly as to the proper meaning of these words, but it seems that you would absolutely leave the legislation of this parliament in such a maze of complications that no one could tell where they were, no one would care to accept any charter, and no one would ask for any privilege for fear he might find himself absolutely ruined by attempting to exercise it. I would think, off-hand, that if it is the opinion of parliament that the law as it stands to-day with respect to liabilities of railway companies in reference to such cases as my hon. friend has in his mind, ought to be changed, modified or reconsidered in some form, it would be equally within the competence of parliament to do it, and would more surely prove that the Act which my hon. friend from St. John and Iberville (Mr. Demers) has introduced would provide a remedy. I have not examined his Bill, but I heard what has fallen from hon. members who have spoken upon it, I do not know how far parliament ought to go in respect to that, therefore I reserve my opinion upon it. It seems to me that we can see where we are going in the case of 301
the Bill of my hon. friend from Iberville, but we cannot see where we are going in the Bill of my hon. friend opposite.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I considered when this Bill was. first introduced that it was one of the most serious pieces of legislation that we were called upon to deal with. It is legislation fraught with the most serious consequences, if it were placed on our statutes. In effect, what is it that this amendment to the Interpretation Act asks us to do ? It asks us to declare that when we confer upon a corporation that we have a right to bring Into existence, certain powers and privileges, that corporation can only exercise those powers and privileges subject to the legislation of the provinces over which we have absolutely no control. Now to state the case in that way is to show the importance of the legislation.
That is, so fains civil liabilities are concerned.

Yes, that would be the anomalous position that we would take, the anomalous legislation we would be responsible for, if the parliament of Canada were to declare that a corporation should have a right to do a thing, or if we enjoined upon a corporation to do a certain thing, and then we were to confer upon a province a right to declare that that which we empowered the corporation to do, was an actionable wrong. One does not require to go any further than to state that. Take, for instance, the case of a railway company connecting two or more provinces together. In order that that railway company might get its charter it will be forced to come here and get legislation from us; and in our legislation we would say that they had a right to operate within these provinces. Our legislation provides as to the equipment of that railway, as to the mode of protecting of rights and property of the public which that railway has to adopt. But the very moment that railway company went into operation, if this Bill were passed into law, when that railway company operated in different provinces, each province would have a right to say : You shall not operate that railway except subject to the conditions we impose upon you. Where would that lead us ? Is it conceivable that we would pass such legislation as that ? I do not mean to discuss the matter any further than to show what the consequences of such legislation would be.
I said a moment ago, in answer to a remark that fell from the hon. leader of the opposition, that the moment you concede the right of the Dominion parliament in a proper case to interfere with civil rights in a province, that very moment you concede that the judgment of the Privy Council in Roy and the Canadian Pacific Railway was

a proper judgment. And what is the reason for it ? The code of the province of Quebec upon which so much reliance has been placed, is only a statute, and the provincial legislature can amend it in respect to those things upon which it has a right to legislate, it can amend it either by direct legislation or inferentially. And with respect to those matters over which we have control and with which we have a right to interfere, we can amend the code, and we are doing it all the time. When we give a railway company the right to operate in a province and say that that corporation shall be exempted from liability provided it compiles with certain requirements, we are within our constitutional rights. I never could understand the reason of the judgment upon which the Court of Appeals-I say if. with all due respect-rendered judgment in this case. They talk about sic utere tuo ut aliemum non laedas. That is a principle of law applicable to the common law of England as well as to our own, and if you are authorized to do a thing by this parliament, you cannot be held to have done that which will make you liable for damages. If this parliament authorizes the doing of a thing, and says to you :	We confer upon you authority to do so and so, on what principle of law can you be held responsible for damages for exercising that right which we confer upon you ? It seems to me I need not go further in the discussion of this case of Roy and the Canadian Pacific Railway. At one time that case was considered in our province as of the highest importance, far reaching in its consequences and as an infringement upon the rights of our provinces in respect to civil rights. Perhaps it may be impertinence on my part, but, not agreeing with that view, I ventured to write an article in one of our legal papers to which the member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) referred, so that I need not weary the House by repeating what I said there.

In stating that there might be legislation which would remedy the condition of affairs brought about by this decision of the Privy Council, of course, I am not considering whether the Quebec decisions are right or wrong. What I venture to suggest and what I believe to be right is that the parliament of Canada in incorporating any railway company may say this : The company may build a line between two given points, it may operate that line, but in so far as the province of Quebec is concerned, if it creates any damage by fire through its engines it shall be responsible to the same extent as if it had not received the protection of this statute.
There is no doubt about that.
It can limit the extent to which the civil liability is incurred.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext: I do not understand my hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Plalifax) to intimate that he would be taken as approving of any such legislation.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I am not discussing the policy of the legislation. I am merely discussing the power of this parliament. In other words, I am stating what is tlie simple fact that this parliament, having power to go to the utmost extent in regard to civil rights, need not go to such an extent, but can go only half way, dr not at all, and so the civil liability would still remain.

I may say that I have no special desire to see this particular Bill passed, but 1 do not think the legislation is of such an extraordinary character as tlie hon. Minister of Justice indicates. The point raised by the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals and by the hon. member for Halifax, strikes me as being a very important one; that is to say, that this legislation is too comprehensive. It is the first time that the point has been indicated to me. The hon. Minister of Justice has never mentioned or indicated it before, but I may say that just such legislation as my hon. friend from Halifax pointed out a moment ago as being within the purview of this legislature has already bean enacted in this parliament. The Railway Act, to give an instance of it, section 288, speaking of the results of the inspection of railways as regards civil liability, says. I do not want to read the whole section :
No inspection had under this Act

in any manner or way to lessen such liability or responsibility of any such company, under the laws in force in the province in which such liability or responsibility crises.
That is an example of legislation which is, I think, quite within our powers exactly on the lines mentioned as possible by the lion. Minister of Railways and Canals, and if the Bill now under consideration in this House lias a fault it is the fault of going too far, as has been indicated, but it is on tlie same lines as section 288 of the statute.
I agree with the hon. gentleman that it is on the same lines; yet, the extent to which that Act goes is clear. It states just exactly the ground it wants to cover and it stops there.
speakername: The . MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND  CANALS@

speechtext: The effect of article 288 is exactly to produce the effect which the hon. Minister of Justice considered as an absurdity, because, that section, as I read it. says : Whatever may be the inspection made your liability as a railway company will remain what it ought to be under the civil law of the province.
Read what the Privy Council says on that section at page 231 of the report of the Roy case.

I will in a minute. I am reasoning on the section as I understand it irrespective of wliat the Privy Council may have decided. I submit that under that section the province of Ontario, or the province of Quebec, by their legislatures, may impose any kind of liability on a railway. Is that not the case ?
I do not think so.
speakername: Tile MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It may be within its sphere because the Privy Council decided a very long time ago in a case of which I forget the title at the present moment that there is a division of the field and that when the parliament of Canada is within its powers and exercises these powers it may exercise them to the fullest extent in order to carry out the object of its creation to a certain extent invading the provincial powers.

Does my hon. friend not see that the section is framed for the purpose of rendering it impossible for any party to contend that because there has been an inspection and that inspection has produced certain results, or certain conclusions have been arrived at, the fact of these conclusions having been arrived at-
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Relieves him from responsibility.
No, it does not either enhance or diminish the liability that the railway company would be subject to if the inspection had not been made.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I understand that the object of that enactment in the Railway Act to which I refer is to stop the railway company from saying : AVe have been inspected, this is the result, and therefore, we are not liable to damages.
Yes, that is the object.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILAVAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Well, on the same lines, in the case of Roy, the railway company said : AVe have been authorized by the statutes of the Dominion of Canada to operate this railway and whatever may be the law in the province of Quebec in regard to torts, or damages, this statute of the Dominion of Canada protects us. That is the way I understand it and the object of this Bill, although I admit it may be too comprehensive, is to declare that no enactment of the Dominion parliament will have the effect of exercising a right conferred by the Dominion parliament from liability under the common law of the province or any Act of the legislature within the powers of the legislature. Of course, if you suppose a case such as the hon. Minister of Justice supposed a moment ago of a statute of the province of Quebec nullifying an enactment of the Dominion parliament in respect to
railways over which it has control, that enactment in the provincial legislature would be ultra vires, would be beyond its powers, because, under the Constitutional Act we have control here over certain railways in the matter of legislation. Under the decision of the Privy Council and which effect the jurisprudence of our courts in regard to railways to the fullest extent that might be necessary in order that we might fully exercise our powers under section 91 of the Confederation Act. But, we cannot go beyond.
I submit that we cannot enact in the parliament of Canada, the Bill which my hon. friend (Mr. Demers, Iberville) has before the House, because we would then be legislating the question of civil rights which is reserved exclusively to the provinces. If the Bill of my hon. friend should become law, there would be a different kind of liability in the English provinces for railway companies from what there is for individuals. There would be a special liability for railway companies enacted by this parliament, which would not be the civil law of the province. The difficulty I find in the Bill of my hon. friend is that it invades the provincial domain, although at first sight it would seem to be far the simplest way to remedy the evil. The judges of the Privy Council declared that the civil law of the province of Quebec applied in this case of Roy, but they interpreted it differently from the interpretation given to it hitherto in all countries which are governed by the principles of the old French law. There is no doubt in my mind that they were right in finding that the principle which must apply in this case is the principle of our provincial law, and if the legislation suggested by my hon. friend (Mr. Demers, Iberville) became law, it would be contrary to the jurisprudence of the Privy Council in the case of Roy, and the generally accepted jurisprudence, that it would be an invasion of the provincial domain of legislation. These are the words in this Act to which exception has been taken on the ground that they are too comprehensive:
No enactments ot the parliament of Canada shall exempt any person exercising a right, power or privilege under a Dominion slatute, from any liability incurred by him under any Act of the legislature or uuder the common law.
It is certainly of a very general character, but I think that it must be understood in the sense in which it has been intended and has stood upon our statute-books for a very .long time. Under section 288, of the Railway Act, nothing shall exempt a person holding powers from this legislature from liability under the common law of the province or any Act of the legislature, in so far as the common law will apply, or the Act of legislature is within the power of the legislature. No man would pretend that it would be in the power of the legislature to enact laws nullifying intra vires enact-

ments of our parliament here. I do not think that any such Act of the provincial legislature would be considered constitutional. The difficulty is the division of the field of legislation between the two powers. If there was no division of the field, the Bill presented by my hon. friend (Mr. Demers, Iberville) would be a very much simpler way to remedy the crying evil which exists in the other provinces where there is no doubt whatever that the decision in the case of Roy would properly apply. But the difficulty in this case is that it is a question of civil law, and I submit that the furthest that we can go is to declare that no empowering enactment passed here ; not only in regard to railway companies but in regard to any enterprise whatever which this parliament has the power to regulate, shall be construed as exempting the party exercising that power from the control of the legislature in so far as that control may be exercised, or from the common law of the province in so far as that common law may apply ; and it can only apply as restricted by the provisions of our Confederation Act.
